definition: Cordial means warm, friendly, and heartfelt in a courteous way — real warmth carried by good manners.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word cordial. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know cordial should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Their rivalry on the tennis tour is famous, but at the net the two champions are unfailingly cordial — warm words, real smiles, and a handshake that lingers.
Polite is weaker than cordial: politeness follows the forms correctly and can stay stone cold, while cordial manners carry real warmth from the heart.
Effusive is stronger than cordial: cordial warmth stays measured and courteous, while effusive greetings gush and overflow past anything the occasion asked for.

Genial is sunny good cheer that belongs to a person's own temperament — a genial man beams at everyone. Cordial names the warmth shown between people, and it can hold even where the two have every reason to be cold.
Gracious is courtesy with generosity in it, flowing naturally from a host or from whoever holds the higher position. Cordial is that same warmth exchanged on equal footing.

The town's two rival bakeries have settled into a wary concord, each keeping to its own side of the square.
Cordial means warm, friendly, and heartfelt in a courteous way — real warmth carried by good manners.

When the visiting team's bus broke down in a snowstorm, the home coach's welcome was cordial in the fullest sense: hot soup in the cafeteria, a warm gym to stretch in, and a handshake for every player who would be trying to beat his squad the next evening.
The warmth is real — soup, shelter, handshakes — and it flows through simple courtesies toward people he has every competitive reason to keep at arm's length.
That heartfelt friendliness, delivered politely and without gush, is what cordial describes.

Cordial does a job its neighbors in this unit can't: affable and amiable describe a person's easy friendliness, and amicable describes dealings free of conflict, but cordial names warmth delivered through courtesy — and it shines brightest between people who owe each other nothing more than politeness.
That's why diplomats keep 'cordial relations,' and why a cordial handshake between rivals means something.
You may also meet the noun: a cordial was once a drink to strengthen the heart.

The two border posts sit fifty meters apart, flying flags of countries that have argued over the valley for a century.
The governments exchange stiff notes every spring.
The guards exchange coffee.
Sergeant Baida carries a thermos across on cold mornings; Corporal Anders sends back honey from his father's hives.
Visiting journalists expecting a tense standoff instead find relations at the checkpoint entirely cordial: warm greetings by name, real laughter, and inquiries after each other's children.
The treaty may be frozen, the guards like to say, but the coffee never is.
